title: A Different Plan
focus: 比较交付方案，提出可讨论的分阶段试点
story:
Daniel writes the names of all the community learning centres across the whiteboard. There are more than I can comfortably hold in my head. Under them, he draws one long line and writes 'same week?'

The question mark is small. I keep looking at it.

The notification repair has completed its additional review. We have corrected another minor logging issue and recorded the test results. The system is more reliable than it was, but my confidence has not returned at the same speed.

“We need a plan to discuss with Elena,” Daniel says. “Not another list of things we might do.”

Rui turns his pen between his fingers. “The centres have different class schedules. Doing everything in one week will make support busy.”

“It also limits how long we maintain two ways of working,” Daniel says.

I have written a suggestion in my notebook. The words look reasonable there, where nobody can disagree with them.

“What if we started with one centre?” I ask.

Daniel looks at me. “As a pilot?”

“Yes. A limited pilot. We could watch the actual work more closely and find problems before involving all the centres.”

“And how long would that take?”

“I don't know yet. We'd need to agree what we're trying to learn and how the centre would take part.”

Daniel leans back. “I'm willing to consider it, but we can't keep calling uncertainty a plan.”

I close the notebook halfway, then open it again.

“Could I compare the options for the client discussion? Including the extra work a pilot creates?”

He considers this. “By tomorrow afternoon. Keep it short.”

Rui and I take the small meeting room after lunch. Instead of starting with a presentation, we draw the current staff journey: find the class, change the record, tell learners, check whether anyone needs more help.

“Whose job is this last part?” I ask.

“Probably centre staff.”

Rui turns my notebook round. “Let's try it. I'll be a tutor. You're on the desk. My room's full of chairs with wet paint. I need the other room.”

“That's a very strange centre.”

“Excellent chairs. Terrible planning.”

I change the room on a sheet of paper. He holds out his hand for the other sheet. I haven't touched it.

“Somebody at your old desk still thinks I'm teaching among the chairs,” he says.

We try again. This time I remember both sheets, but when he asks which one I changed first I can't tell. It takes thirty seconds for two people who made up the problem to lose track of it.

I cross out easy to manage. Under the three choices I write what each would ask of a person alone at a desk. If we introduce the system everywhere, everybody learns at once. If we wait, everybody keeps doing today's work. If we choose one centre, somebody there becomes the link between two ways of working. I can give Daniel the choices. I don't know the name of the person who would have to live with the third one.

In the afternoon, we test another sequence of changes and a temporary notification failure. The system records what happened, but it cannot tell us whether a learner has read an email. I add that limitation to the draft.

Rui reads over it. “Don't promise that fewer centres means fewer problems.”

“Fewer people exposed to the first problems?”

“If the scope really stays limited.”

I change the sentence.

The next day, I sit opposite Daniel with a single printed page. He reads it without speaking. I resist the urge to explain every line before he reaches it.

“You've put staff time under every option,” he says.

“It belongs under every option.”

“Fair.” He taps the pilot column. “Who chooses the centre?”

“Elena and the centre, I think. We can explain the technical requirements, but we don't know their workload.”

“What would make us stop?”

I show him a short list of proposed conditions: incorrect times, wrong recipients, or a failure staff cannot handle through an agreed fallback. None of the conditions is approved yet. We also need a reliable way to return to the existing process without losing changes.

Daniel draws a line under that point.

“That's not a small detail.”

“No. We'd have to test it and agree who makes the decision.”

He looks out through the glass wall. Someone is carrying a monitor past, walking backwards while a colleague holds the other end.

“All right,” he says. “Let's evaluate the one-centre approach with Elena. I'm not approving a launch date today.”

“I'll make that clear in the notes.”

“And send her the alternatives. She may have reasons we haven't considered.”

At the printer I find my first diagram lying face up. One centre is a little square. I try putting my thumb over it. A whole building disappears.

Rui comes up behind me. “Are you doing magic?”

“Bad magic. I can make London vanish.”

“Can you make the printer work?”

Its red light is on. We open the tray and find the back of my proposal folded like a fan. When I pull it straight the line about extra staff is almost impossible to read. I write it in again with his pen.

That is the copy I keep. Elena gets the clean version, including the option to wait. Half an hour later a reply arrives. She can give us twenty minutes between the end of one class and the start of another. There is no comment about the plan. For the first time it occurs to me that those twenty minutes already belong to somebody.

phrases.en: What if we started with one centre?
phrases.zh: 提出可讨论的替代方案

phrases.en: We need to include the extra work.
That depends on the agreed scope.
We haven’t approved a launch date.
phrases.zh: 防止把评估误解为上线承诺

practice.grammar: 用 What if + 过去式提出试探性建议：What if we started with one centre? 这里 started 表示较委婉的设想，不是在讲过去发生的事情。
practice.pronunciation: 练习让建议自然收尾：What if we started / with ONE centre? 在 started 后短停，强调 ONE。再说 We need to include / the EXTRA work，用重音提醒听者也要考虑成本。

questions.q: What extra work could a pilot create?
questions.a: Someone would need to coordinate two processes and keep the records consistent.

questions.q: What do the two sheets help Andy notice?
questions.a: One person could change a room in one record and forget the other.

questions.q: Why should Elena and the centre help choose the pilot location?
questions.a: They understand the centre’s workload better than the engineering team does.

roleplay.context: 你是 Andy，向 Daniel 提出单个中心试点，必须同时说明代价与未知信息。

turns.line: Why not introduce it everywhere in the same week?
turns.cue: 比较同时支持多个中心的压力与小范围试点的价值。

turns.line: A pilot sounds like extra work for everyone.
turns.cue: 承认双流程和记录一致性的成本，不把方案说成没有代价。

turns.line: So can I announce the launch date?
turns.cue: 说明目前只同意评估，还需客户参与和明确停止条件。

practice.transfer: 你建议团队试用一个新的会议方式。用英语比较“全团队立即采用”“一个小组先试”“暂缓”三个选项，各说一个好处和一个成本，最后提出需要了解的问题。
practice.retell: 用两分钟向没有读过故事的人解释提案。先说问题，再比较三个方案，最后明确当前决定和仍待客户确认的事项；不要说项目已上线。

translations.18-1: Daniel在白板上写下了所有社区学习中心的名字。
translations.18-2: 数量多得让我很难全记在脑子里。
translations.18-3: 他在名字下面画了一条长线，又写上“同一周？”
translations.18-6: 通知功能的修复已经完成了追加评审。
translations.18-7: 我们又修正了一个小的日志问题，并记录了测试结果。
translations.18-8: 系统比以前可靠了，但我的信心没有恢复得那么快。
translations.18-9: “我们需要一个能拿去和Elena讨论的方案。”Daniel说。
translations.18-10: “不能又是一张列着各种可能做法的清单。”
translations.18-12: “各个中心的课程安排不一样。
translations.18-13: 全挤在一周里，支持工作会很忙。”
translations.18-14: “但这样也能缩短同时维护两套工作方式的时间。”Daniel说。
translations.18-15: 我已经在笔记本上写下了一个建议。
translations.18-16: 写在本子上时，那些话显得很有道理，毕竟没人能在那里反驳。
translations.18-17: “要不先从一个中心开始？”我问。
translations.18-21: 做一个范围有限的试点。
translations.18-22: 这样我们能更近距离地观察实际工作，在所有中心参与之前发现问题。”
translations.18-25: 我们得先商定想从中了解什么，以及中心如何参与。”
translations.18-27: “我愿意考虑，但我们不能总把不确定的想法叫作计划。”
translations.18-28: 我把笔记本合上一半，又重新打开。
translations.18-29: “我能不能先比较一下几个方案，供客户讨论时参考？
translations.18-30: 也包括试点会带来的额外工作。”
translations.18-34: 午饭后，我和Rui去了小会议室。
translations.18-35: 我们没有先做演示文稿，而是画出工作人员目前的操作流程：找到课程、修改记录、通知学员，再检查是否有人需要进一步帮助。
translations.18-38: Rui把我的笔记本转了过来。
translations.18-42: 我的教室里全是油漆还没干的椅子。
translations.18-47: 我在一张纸上改了教室。
translations.18-50: “照你们前台原来的记录，我还在那堆椅子中间上课呢。”他说。
translations.18-52: 这回我记得两张都改，可他一问先改的是哪张，我就答不上来。
translations.18-53: 才三十秒，连编出这道题的我们俩都理不清了。
translations.18-54: 我划掉“容易管理”四个字。
translations.18-55: 我在三个方案下分别写上，如果前台只有一个人，各个方案会给这个人带来什么活儿。
translations.18-56: 如果各处同时上线，所有人就都得同时学。
translations.18-57: 如果等等再说，大家就继续照今天的办法做事。
translations.18-58: 如果只选一个中心，就得靠那里的某个人把两套做法接起来。
translations.18-60: 可要是选了第三种，天天得这么做的那个人叫什么，我都不知道。
translations.18-61: 下午，我们又测试了一组连续修改和一次通知暂时发送失败的情况。
translations.18-62: 系统记录了发生的事，却无法告诉我们学员是否读过邮件。
translations.18-63: 我把这个局限加进了草稿。
translations.18-65: “别承诺中心少了，问题就一定少。”
translations.18-66: “那就说，最初出现问题时，受影响的人更少？”
translations.18-69: 第二天，我带着打印好的一页纸，坐在Daniel对面。
translations.18-71: 我忍住了在他读到之前就逐行解释的冲动。
translations.18-72: “每个方案下面，你都写了工作人员的时间投入。”他说。
translations.18-73: “每个方案都需要考虑这一项。”
translations.18-78: 我们可以说明技术要求，但不了解他们的工作量。”
translations.18-80: 我给他看了一份简短的建议条件清单：时间错误、收件人错误，或出现工作人员无法通过约定的备用流程处理的故障。
translations.18-81: 这些条件还没有得到批准。
translations.18-82: 我们还需要一种可靠的方式，在不丢失修改的情况下退回现有流程。
translations.18-83: Daniel在这一点下面画了一条线。
translations.18-86: 我们得测试它，还要商定谁有权作这个决定。”
translations.18-87: 他透过玻璃墙向外看去。
translations.18-88: 有人正倒退着搬运一台显示器，同事托着另一端。
translations.18-90: “我们和Elena一起评估单个中心的方案。
translations.18-91: 今天我不会批准上线日期。”
translations.18-94: 她可能有我们没考虑到的理由。”
translations.18-95: 我在打印机旁看见我的第一张图，正面朝上。
translations.18-96: 一个小方框就代表一所中心。
translations.18-98: 一整栋楼就这么消失了。
translations.18-105: 我们拉开纸盘，发现提案的背页已经折成了一把扇子。
translations.18-106: 我把纸展开，需要额外人手的那一行几乎认不出来了。
translations.18-107: 我借他的笔，把那行字又写了一遍。
translations.18-109: 我给Elena的是整洁的那份，里面也列着暂缓的选项。
translations.18-111: 一堂课结束到下一堂开始之间，她可以给我们二十分钟。
translations.18-113: 我头一回想到，这二十分钟原本也是有人要用的。
